title: Sun, Moon, and stars
keyIdea: The sky has patterns we can predict. Every day the Sun comes up in the east, is high at midday and goes down in the west. Stars come out when the sky is dark; in the day they are still there, but the bright sky hides them. The Moon's shape changes a little each night: from new moon it grows to full moon, then shrinks back, and the pattern starts again about once a month. The Moon is often in the day sky too.
familyTip: Keep a Moon diary for two weeks: each clear evening, step outside and draw the Moon's shape in a box on a calendar. Note where the Sun goes down from your window. Ask: what shape will the Moon be next week? Then check.

visual.caption: Is it a pattern we see every day, or one that takes about a month? Drag each card, or tap it and then tap a box.

items: The Sun comes up in the east
The Moon goes from new to full and back
The Sun goes down in the west
Stars come out when it gets dark
The Moon is a thin crescent again

lab.caption: Flagship lab: move the Sun east to west, turn day into night, step a month of Moon shapes, order them and sort the sky.

kid: The Sun comes up in the morning. We call that sunrise. It comes up in the east. It is high in the sky at midday. In the evening it goes down in the west. That is sunset. It happens every day.
Stars come out at night. Where are they in the day? They are still in the sky. The sunny sky is so bright that we cannot see them. When it gets dark, they show.
The Moon looks a bit different each night. First we see a thin slice. It grows to a half moon, and then to a full round moon. Then it shrinks back. This takes about a month, and then it starts again.
You can often see the Moon in the day too. It is not just a night thing. Look up on the way to school and you may spot a pale half moon.
adult: Ages 6 to 7. This is NGSS 1-ESS1-1, use observations of the sun, moon and stars to describe patterns that can be predicted, with the Patterns crosscutting concept. It also fits Year 1 seasonal change in the National Curriculum in England. Key words: sunrise, sunset, east, west, pattern, predict, new moon, crescent, half moon, full moon, month.

At this age the goal is observing and predicting patterns, not explaining their causes. The Sun only seems to move across the sky because Earth turns; it rises roughly in the east and sets roughly in the west, exactly so only near the equinoxes. Moon phases come from seeing more or less of the Moon's sunlit half, and the cycle takes about 29.5 days. The lab shows the waxing Moon lit on the right, as seen from the Northern Hemisphere.

Common mistakes: thinking stars go away or switch off in the day; thinking the Moon is only out at night; expecting the Moon to change from new to full overnight, or to take a whole year; and thinking the Sun sets where it rose. Some children also think the shape change is a cloud or Earth's shadow covering the Moon; that comes later, but avoid saying it.

In the lab your child drags the Sun from sunrise to sunset, turns a day sky into night and sees stars appear, steps through 30 nights of Moon shapes, puts five shapes in order from new to full, and sorts six sky things into day, night or both. A seasonal link: in summer the Sun sets later, so stars come out later.

practice.prompt: The Sun comes up in the east. Where does it go down?
practice.hint: Think of the Sun moving across the sky to the other side.
practice.explain: Every day the Sun comes up in the east and goes down in the west, on the other side of the sky.

practice.prompt: The Moon shapes take about 30 days to come round. There have been {a} days since the full moon. How many more days until the next full moon?
practice.hint: The whole pattern is about 30 days. Take away the {a} days that have gone.
practice.explain: 30 − {a} = {=30-a}. In about {=30-a} more days, the full moon comes back.

practice.prompt: Where are the stars at midday?
choices: Still in the sky, hidden by the bright sky
practice.hint: Do stars really go away, or can we just not see them?
practice.explain: Stars are always there. The bright day sky hides them. When it gets dark, we can see them.

practice.prompt: Mia started her Moon diary at new moon, {a} nights ago. The whole pattern takes about 30 nights. About how many more nights until the next new moon?
practice.hint: The pattern is about 30 nights long. Take away the {a} nights already drawn.
practice.explain: 30 − {a} = {=30-a}, so the next new moon is about {=30-a} nights away.

practice.prompt: Last night was a thin crescent Moon. What will it look like in a few nights?
practice.hint: After new moon, the lit part grows a little each night.
practice.explain: The crescent grows a little each night, to a half moon in about a week.

pool.prompt: Which comes first after a new moon?
pool.hint: The lit part grows a little at a time.
pool.explain: New moon, then a thin crescent, then a half moon, then nearly full, then full.

pool.prompt: Can you see the Moon in the day?
pool.hint: Think of a pale Moon in a blue sky.
pool.explain: The Moon is in the day sky on many days. It looks pale because the sky is bright.

pool.prompt: The Moon goes from new moon to full moon in about 15 days. It is day {a} after new moon. About how many days until full moon?
pool.hint: Full moon is about day 15. Take away the {a} days that have already gone.
pool.explain: 15 − {a} = {=15-a}. In about {=15-a} days the Moon will be full.

pool.prompt: Why do we not see stars at lunch time?
choices: They switch off in the day
pool.hint: Can you see a torch in bright sunshine?
pool.explain: Stars are still there. Like a torch in sunshine, they are too faint to see against the bright sky.

pool.prompt: Mia sees the Sun low on the west side of the sky. What time of day is it?
pool.hint: Where does the Sun go down?
pool.explain: The Sun goes down in the west, so low in the west means it is evening, near sunset.

choices: new moon, crescent, half moon, full moon
full moon, new moon, half moon, crescent
half moon, full moon, crescent, new moon
pool.hint: Start with no light and add a little each time.
pool.explain: From new moon the lit part grows: crescent, then half, then full.

pool.prompt: Jo draws the Moon every night for {w} weeks. How many Moon pictures does she draw?
pool.hint: A week has 7 nights. Count {w} lots of 7.
pool.explain: {w} weeks × 7 nights = {=7*w} pictures, enough to see the Moon change shape.

pool.prompt: In summer the Sun goes down late. When do the stars come out?
choices: At the same time as in winter
pool.hint: Stars show when the sky is dark.
pool.explain: In summer it gets dark later, so the stars come out later than in winter.
